title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 364
paragraphs: Such is this labyrinth; but an even greater wonder is offered by the lake called the Lake of Moiris, along whose side this labyrinth was built. The measure of its circumference is three thousand six hundred furlongs (sixty schoines), which is the same number of furlongs as the extent of Egypt itself along the sea. The lake lies stretched lengthwise from north to south, and at its deepest it is fifty fathoms deep. That this lake is artificial and dug by hand is obvious, for in about the middle of the lake stand two pyramids, each rising fifty fathoms above the water, with the same height built below the water as well; and upon each is set a colossal stone statue seated on a throne. So the pyramids are a hundred fathoms in total height, and these hundred fathoms are equal to a furlong of six hundred feet — the fathom being six feet or four cubits, the feet being four palms each, and the cubits six palms. The water in the lake does not come from the land nearby, for that country is very short of water, but has been brought there from the Nile by a canal: for six months the water flows into the lake, and for six months out again into the Nile. Whenever the water flows out, it brings into the royal treasury a talent of silver a day from the fish caught, and twenty pounds a day when the water is flowing in.
